entries.c100ff450d072089ffc589c07b791fada52ac679: <div sID="gen11260" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="47" osisID="Ps.47" sID="Ps.47"/> <div eID="gen11260" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11261" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen11262" type="x-p"/> The scope of this psalm is to stir us up to praise God, to stir up all people to do so; and, I. We are directed in what manner to do it, publicly, cheerfully, and intelligently, <reference osisRef="Ps.47.1">ver. 1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.47.6">6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.47.7">7</reference>. II. We are furnished with matter for praise. 1. God's majesty, <reference osisRef="Ps.47.2">ver. 2</reference>. 2. His sovereign and universal dominion, <reference osisRef="Ps.47.2">ver. 2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.47.7-Ps.47.9">7-9</reference>. 3. The great things he had done, and will do, for his people, <reference osisRef="Ps.47.3-Ps.47.5">ver. 3-5</reference>. Many suppose that this psalm was penned upon occasion of the bringing up of the ark to Mount Zion which <reference osisRef="Ps.47.5">ver. 5</reference> seems to refer to ("God has gone up with a shout");—but it looks further, to the ascension of Christ into the heavenly Zion, after he had finished his undertaking on earth, and to the setting up of his kingdom in the world, to which the heathen should become willing subjects. In singing this psalm we are to give honour to the exalted Redeemer, to rejoice in his exaltation, and to celebrate his praises, confessing that he is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.
entries.a4f1b3c95fa7c7d2c9286a08ffcd96a9139125c4: <div eID="gen11262" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen11261" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Exhortation to Praise God.</title> <div sID="gen11263" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> O clap your hands, all ye people; shout unto God with the voice of triumph. <hi type="super">2</hi> For the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> most high <hi type="italic">is</hi> terrible; <hi type="italic">he is</hi> a great King over all the earth. <hi type="super">3</hi> He shall subdue the people under us, and the nations under our feet. <hi type="super">4</hi> He shall choose our inheritance for us, the excellency of Jacob whom he loved. Selah. <div eID="gen11263" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11264" type="x-p"/> The psalmist, having his own heart filled with great and good thoughts of God, endeavours to engage all about him in the blessed work of praise, as one convinced that God is worthy of all blessing and praise, and as one grieved at his own and others' backwardness to and barrenness in this work. Observe, in these verses, <div eID="gen11264" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11265" type="x-p"/> I. Who are called upon to praise God: "<hi type="italic">All you people,</hi> all you people of Israel;" those were his own subjects, and under his charge, and therefore he will engage them to praise God, for on them he has an influence. Whatever others do, he and his house, he and his people, shall praise the Lord. Or, "All you people and nations of the earth;" and so it may be taken as a prophecy of the conversion of the Gentiles and the bringing of them into the church; see <reference osisRef="Rom.15.11">Rom. xv. 11</reference>. <div eID="gen11265" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11266" type="x-p"/> II. What they are called upon to do: "<hi type="italic">O clap your hands,</hi> in token of your own joy and satisfaction in what God has done for you, of your approbation, nay, your admiration, of what God has done in general, and of your indignation against all the enemies of God's glory, <reference osisRef="Job.27.23">Job xxvii. 23</reference>. <hi type="italic">Clap your hands,</hi> as men transported with pleasure, that cannot contain themselves; <hi type="italic">shout unto God,</hi> not to make him hear (his ear is not heavy), but to make all about you hear, and take notice how much you are affected and filled with the works of God. Shout <hi type="italic">with the voice of triumph</hi> in him, and in his power and goodness, that others may join with you in the triumph." Note, Such expressions of pious and devout affections as to some may seem indecent and imprudent ought not to be hastily censured and condemned, much less ridiculed, because, if they come from an upright heart, God will accept the strength of the affection and excuse the weakness of the expressions of it. <div eID="gen11266" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11267" type="x-p"/> III. What is suggested to us as matter for our praise. 1. That the God with whom we have to do is a God of awful majesty (<reference osisRef="Ps.47.2">v. 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">The Lord most high is terrible.</hi> He is infinitely above the noblest creatures, higher than the highest; there are those perfections in him that are to be reverenced by all, and particularly that power, holiness, and justice, that are to be dreaded by all those that contend with him. 2. That he is a God of sovereign and universal dominion. He is a King that reigns alone, and with an absolute power, <hi type="italic">a King over all the earth;</hi> all the creatures, being made by him, are subject to him, and therefore he is <hi type="italic">a great King,</hi> the King of kings. 3. That he takes a particular care of his people and their concerns, has done so and ever will; (1.) In giving them victory and success (<reference osisRef="Ps.47.3">v. 3</reference>), subduing the people and nations under them, both those that stood in their way (<reference osisRef="Ps.44.2">Ps. xliv. 2</reference>) and those that made attempts upon them. This God had done for them, witness the planting of them in Canaan, and their continuance there unto this day. This they doubted not but he would still do for them by his servant David, who prospered which way soever he turned his victorious arms. But this looks forward to the kingdom of the Messiah, which was to be set over all the earth, and not confined to the Jewish nation. Jesus Christ shall subdue the Gentiles; he shall bring <hi type="italic">them in as sheep into the fold</hi> (so the word signifies), not for slaughter, but for preservation. He shall subdue their affections, and make them a <hi type="italic">willing people in the day of his power,</hi> shall bring their thoughts into obedience to him, and reduce those who had gone astray, under the guidance of the <hi type="italic">great shepherd and bishop of souls,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.25">1 Pet. ii. 25</reference>. (2.) In giving them rest and settlement (<reference osisRef="Ps.47.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">He shall choose our inheritance for us.</hi> He had chosen the land of Canaan to be an inheritance for Israel; it was the land which the Lord their God spied out for them; see <reference osisRef="Deut.32.8">Deut. xxxii. 8</reference>. This justified their possession of that land, and gave them a good title; and this sweetened their enjoyment of it, and made it comfortable; they had reason to think it a happy lot, and to be satisfied in it, when it was that which Infinite Wisdom chose for them. And the setting up of God's sanctuary in it made it <hi type="italic">the excellency,</hi> the honour, <hi type="italic">of Jacob</hi> (<reference osisRef="Amos.6.8">Amos vi. 8</reference>); and he chose so good an inheritance for Jacob because he loved him, <reference osisRef="Deut.7.8">Deut. vii. 8</reference>. Apply this spiritually, and it bespeaks, [1.] The happiness of the saints, that God himself has chosen their inheritance for them, and it is a goodly heritage: <hi type="italic">he</hi> has chosen it who knows the soul, and what will serve to make it happy; and he has chosen so well that he himself has undertaken to be the <hi type="italic">inheritance of his people</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.16.5">Ps. xvi. 5</reference>), and he has laid up for them in the other world an inheritance incorruptible, <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.4">1 Pet. i. 4</reference>. This will be indeed the excellency of Jacob, for whom, because he loved them, he prepared such a happiness as eye has not seen. [2.] The faith and submission of the saints to God. This is the language of every gracious soul, "God shall choose my inheritance for me; let him appoint me my lot, and I will acquiesce in the appointment. He knows what is good for me better than I do for myself, and therefore I will have no will of my own but what is resolved into his."
entries.c3ffa104ea021bdc688550629a840a4840d74364: <div eID="gen11267" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Exhortation to Praise God.</title> <div sID="gen11268" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">5</hi> God is gone up with a shout, the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> with the sound of a trumpet. <hi type="super">6</hi> Sing praises to God, sing praises: sing praises unto our King, sing praises. <hi type="super">7</hi> For God <hi type="italic">is</hi> the King of all the earth: sing ye praises with understanding. <hi type="super">8</hi> God reigneth over the heathen: God sitteth upon the throne of his holiness. <hi type="super">9</hi> The princes of the people are gathered together, <hi type="italic">even</hi> the people of the God of Abraham: for the shields of the earth <hi type="italic">belong</hi> unto God: he is greatly exalted. <div eID="gen11268" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11269" type="x-p"/> We are here most earnestly pressed to praise God, and to sing his praises; so backward are we to this duty that we have need to be urged to it by precept upon precept, and line upon line; so we are here (<reference osisRef="Ps.47.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">Sing praises to God,</hi> and again, <hi type="italic">Sing praises, Sing praises to our King,</hi> and again, <hi type="italic">Sing praises.</hi> This intimates that it is a very necessary and excellent duty, that it is a duty we ought to be frequent and abundant in; we may sing praises again and again in the same words, and it is no vain repetition if it be done with new affections. Should not a people praise their God? <reference osisRef="Dan.5.4">Dan. v. 4</reference>. Should not subjects praise their king? God is our God, our King, and therefore we must praise him; we must sing his praises, as those that are pleased with them and that are not ashamed of them. But here is a needful rule subjoined (<reference osisRef="Ps.47.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">Sing you praises with understanding,</hi> with <hi type="italic">Maschil.</hi> 1. "Intelligently; as those that do yourselves understand why and for what reasons you praise God and what is the meaning of the service." This is the gospel-rule (<reference osisRef="1Cor.14.15">1 Cor. xiv. 15</reference>), <hi type="italic">to sing with the spirit and with the understanding also;</hi> it is only with the heart that we make melody to the Lord, <reference osisRef="Eph.5.19">Eph. v. 19</reference>. It is not an acceptable service if it be not a reasonable service. 2. "Instructively, as those that desire to make others understand God's glorious perfections, and to teach them to praise him." Three things are mentioned in these verses as just matter for our praises, and each of them will admit of a double sense:— <div eID="gen11269" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11270" type="x-p"/> I. We must praise God going up (<reference osisRef="Ps.47.5">v. 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">God has gone up with a shout,</hi> which may refer, 1. To the carrying up of the ark to the hill of Zion, which was done with great solemnity, David himself dancing before it, the priests, it is likely, blowing the trumpets, and the people following with their loud huzzas. The ark being the instituted token of God's special presence with them, when that was brought up by warrant from him he might be said to <hi type="italic">go up.</hi> The emerging of God's ordinances out of obscurity, in order to the more public and solemn administration of them, is a great favour to any people, which they have reason to rejoice in and give thanks for. 2. To the ascension of our Lord Jesus into heaven, when he had finished his work on earth, <reference osisRef="Acts.1.9">Acts i. 9</reference>. Then <hi type="italic">God went up with a shout,</hi> the shout of a King, of a conqueror, as one who, having <hi type="italic">spoiled principalities and powers,</hi> then <hi type="italic">led captivity captive,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.68.18">Ps. lxviii. 18</reference>. He went up as a Mediator, typified by the ark and the mercy-seat over it, and was brought as the ark was into the most holy place, <hi type="italic">into heaven itself;</hi> see <reference osisRef="Heb.9.24">Heb. ix. 24</reference>. We read not of a shout, or of the sound of a trumpet, at the ascension of Christ, but they were the inhabitants of the upper world, those sons of God, that then shouted for joy, <reference osisRef="Job.38.7">Job xxxviii. 7</reference>. He shall come again in the same manner as he went (<reference osisRef="Acts.1.11">Acts i. 11</reference>) and we are sure that he shall come again with a shout and the sound of a trumpet. <div eID="gen11270" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11271" type="x-p"/> II. We must praise God reigning, <reference osisRef="Ps.47.7-Ps.47.8">v. 7, 8</reference>. God is not only our King, and therefore we owe our homage to him, but he is <hi type="italic">King of all the earth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.47.7">v. 7</reference>), over all the kings of the earth, and therefore in every place the incense of praise is to be offered up to him. Now this may be understood, 1. Of the kingdom of providence. God, as Creator, and the God of nature, <hi type="italic">reigns over the heathen,</hi> disposes of them and all their affairs, as he pleases, though they know him not, nor have any regard to him: <hi type="italic">He sits upon the throne of his holiness,</hi> which he has prepared in the heavens, and there he rules over all, even over the heathen, serving his own purposes by them and upon them. See here the extent of God's government; all are born within his allegiance; even the heathen that serve other gods are ruled by the true God, our God, whether they will or no. See the equity of his government; it is a throne of holiness, on which he sits, whence he gives warrants, orders, and judgment, in which we are sure there is no iniquity. 2. Of the kingdom of the Messiah. Jesus Christ, who is God, and whose <hi type="italic">throne is for ever and ever reigns over the heathen;</hi> not only he is entrusted with the administration of the providential kingdom, but he shall set up the kingdom of his grace in the Gentile world, and rule in the hearts of multitudes that were bred up in heathenism, <reference osisRef="Eph.2.12-Eph.2.13">Eph. ii. 12, 13</reference>. This the apostle speaks of as a great mystery that the <hi type="italic">Gentiles should be fellow-heirs,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.3.6">Eph. iii. 6</reference>. Christ <hi type="italic">sits upon the throne of his holiness,</hi> his throne in the heavens, where all the administrations of his government are intended to show forth God's holiness and to advance holiness among the children of men. <div eID="gen11271" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11272" type="x-p"/> III. We must praise God as attended and honoured by <hi type="italic">the princes of the people,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.47.9">v. 9</reference>. This may be understood, 1. Of the congress or convention of the states of Israel, the heads and rulers of the several tribes, at the solemn feasts, or to despatch the public business of the nation. It was the honour of Israel that they were <hi type="italic">the people of the God of Abraham,</hi> as they were Abraham's seed and taken into his covenant; and, thanks be to God, this blessing of Abraham has come upon the isles of the Gentiles, <reference osisRef="Gal.3.14">Gal. iii. 14</reference>. It was their happiness that they had a settled government, <hi type="italic">princes of their people,</hi> who were the <hi type="italic">shields of their land.</hi> Magistracy is the shield of a nation, and it is a great mercy to any people to have this shield, especially when their princes, <hi type="italic">their shields, belong unto the Lord,</hi> are devoted to his honour, and their power is employed in his service, for then he is greatly exalted. It is likewise the honour of God that, in another sense, the <hi type="italic">shields of the earth do belong to him;</hi> magistracy is his institution, and he serves his own purposes by it in the government of the world, turning the hearts of kings as the rivers of water, which way soever he pleases. It was well with Israel when the princes of their people were gathered together to consult for the public welfare. The unanimous agreement of the great ones of a nation in the things that belong to its peace is a very happy omen, which promises abundance of blessings. 2. It may be applied to the calling of the Gentiles into the church of Christ, and taken as a prophecy that in the days of the Messiah the kings of the earth and their people should join themselves to the church, and bring their glory and power into the New Jerusalem, that they should all become <hi type="italic">the people of the God of Abraham,</hi> to whom it was promised that he should be <hi type="italic">the father of many nations.</hi> The <hi type="italic">volunteers</hi> of the people (so it may be read); it is the same word that is used in <reference osisRef="Ps.110.3">Ps. cx. 3</reference>, <hi type="italic">Thy people shall be willing;</hi> for those that are gathered to Christ are not forced, but made freely willing, to be his. When the <hi type="italic">shields of the earth,</hi> the ensigns of royal dignity (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.14.27-1Kgs.14.28">1 Kings xiv. 27, 28</reference>), are surrendered to the Lord Jesus, as the keys of a city are presented to the conqueror or sovereign, when princes use their power for the advancement of the interests of religion, then Christ is greatly exalted.  <chapter eID="Ps.47"/> <div eID="gen11272" type="x-p"/>

entries.4c573df2391b3df40e0b89d91c8a2c2eae4a3861: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6010"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 47</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.47.1-Ps.47.9">Psa 47:1-9</reference>. Praise is given to God for victory, perhaps that recorded (<reference osisRef="2Chr.20.20-2Chr.20.30">2Ch 20:20-30</reference>); and His dominions over all people, Jews and Gentiles, is asserted.</title> <div sID="gen9160" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6010"/><hi type="bold">1. clap ... hands ... people--</hi>literally, "peoples," or "nations" (compare <reference osisRef="Deut.32.43">De 32:43</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.18.49">Psa 18:49</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.98.9">98:9</reference>). <div eID="gen9160" type="x-p"/>
entries.6e4e3e368deffc947badc7f8be4c3de6ef3c77f2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6011"/><div sID="gen9161" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6011"/>2-3. His universal sovereignty now exists, and will be made known. <div eID="gen9161" type="x-p"/>
entries.c6b57edd87f7227a1e695e357ea3836a291d2b4a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6013"/><div sID="gen9163" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6013"/><hi type="bold">4. He shall ... inheritance--</hi>the heathen to be possessed by His Church (<reference osisRef="Ps.2.8">Psa 2:8</reference>), as Canaan by the Jews.<div eID="gen9163" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9164" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">excellency of Jacob--</hi>literally, "pride," or, that in which he glories (not necessarily, though often, in a bad sense), the privileges of the chosen people--<div eID="gen9164" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9165" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">whom he loved--</hi>His love being the sole cause of granting them. <div eID="gen9165" type="x-p"/>
entries.3eaae944e37bbcd0bedc6fe2fedaf3ae2945c2cf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6014"/><div sID="gen9166" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6014"/>5-7. God, victorious over His enemies, reascends to heaven, amid the triumphant praises of His people, who celebrate His sovereign dominion. This sovereignty is what the Psalm teaches; hence he adds,<div eID="gen9166" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9167" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sing ... praises with understanding--</hi>literally, "sing and play an instructive (Psalm)." The whole typifies Christ's ascension (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.68.18">Psa 68:18</reference>). <div eID="gen9167" type="x-p"/>
entries.8259285292a8a096bd727bdc7ac58fcbbe8d6eff: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6015"/><div sID="gen9168" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6015"/>8-9. The instruction continued.<div eID="gen9168" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9169" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">throne of ... holiness--</hi>or, "holy throne" (see on <reference osisRef="Ps.2.6">Psa 2:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.23.4">Psa 23:4</reference>). <div eID="gen9169" type="x-p"/>

entries.3c403f2adf5c7346f6fac787e2f82ad5af5aab21: <div eID="gen20132" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen20133" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen20134" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20134" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20133" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen20135" type="x-p"/> The Gentiles are invited to celebrate the praises of God as the Sovereign of the world, <reference osisRef="Psa.47.1">Psa 47:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.47.2">Psa 47:2</reference>. The Jews exalt in his kindness to them, <reference osisRef="Psa.47.3">Psa 47:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.47.4">Psa 47:4</reference>. All then join to celebrate his Majesty, as reigniny over the heathen, and gathering the dispersed Jews and Gentiles together into one Church, <reference osisRef="Psa.47.5-Psa.47.9">Psa 47:5-9</reference>. <div eID="gen20135" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20136" type="x-p"/> The title, "A Psalm for the sons of Korah," has nothing remarkable in it. The Psalm was probably written about the same time with the preceding, and relates to the happy state of the Jews when returned to their own land. They renewed their praises and promises of obedienee, and celebrate him for the deliverance they had received. See the introduction to <reference osisRef="Psa.46.1-Psa.46.11">Psa 46:1-11</reference> (note). In a spiritual sense, it appears to relate to the calling of the Gentiles to be made partakers of the blessings of the Gospel with the converted Jews. <div eID="gen20136" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20137" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen20137" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20138" type="x-p"/> O clap your hands, all ye people - Let both Jews and Gentiles magnify the Lord: the Jews, for being delivered from the Babylonish captivity; the Gentiles, for being called to enter into the glorious liberty of the children of God.
entries.ae529d167bfb776ec69464ffa36450bed7480d93: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen20138" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20139" type="x-p"/> For the Lord most high is terrible - He has insufferable majesty, and is a great King - the mightiest of all emperors, for he is Sovereign over the whole earth.
entries.14fd2031af0160319e26896c7f84292b457dc192: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen20139" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20140" type="x-p"/> He shall subdue the people under us - He shall do again for us what he had done for our forefathers - give us dominion over our enemies, and establish us in our own land. I would rather read this in the past tense, relative to what God did for their fathers in destroying the Canaanites, and giving them the promised land for their possession, and taking the people for his own inheritance. This is also applied to the conversion of the Gentiles who, on the rejection of the Jews, have become his inheritance; and whom he has chosen to inherit all those spiritual blessings typified by the sacrifices and other significant rites and ceremonies of the Jewish Church.
entries.9bcefc4e0e7072528920d7272800cd15857c438b: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen20140" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20141" type="x-p"/> God is gone up with a shout - Primarily, this may refer to the rejoicing and sounding of trumpets, when the ark was lifted up to be carried on the shoulders of the Levites. But it is generally understood as a prophetic declaration of the ascension of our Lord Jesus Christ; and the shout may refer to the exultation of the evangelists and apostles in preaching Christ crucified, buried, risen from the dead, and ascended to heaven, ever to appear in the presence of God for us. This was the triumph of the apostles; and the conversion of multitudes of souls by this preaching was the triumph of the cross of Christ.
entries.e68d0d2d302c4c64e4e52483c15d314ca69532e8: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen20141" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20142" type="x-p"/> Sing praises - זמרו zammeru: this word is four times repeated in this short verse, and shows at once the earnestness and happiness of the people. They are the words of exultation and triumph. Feel your obligation to God; express it in thanksgiving: be thankful, be eternally thankful, to God your King.
entries.253cbe5ef23cc9c5801a9e2fd8a3f4497d2433ab: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen20142" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20143" type="x-p"/> For God is the King of all the earth - He is not your King only, but the King of the universe. He has no limited power, no confined dominion. <div eID="gen20143" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20144" type="x-p"/> Sing ye praises with understanding - זמרו משכיל zammeru maskil, sing an instructive song. Let sense and sound go together. Let your hearts and heads go with your voices. Understand what you sing; and feel what you understand; and let the song be what will give instruction in righteousness to them that hear it. Sing wisely - Anglo-Saxon. Multitudes sing foolishly.
entries.7de7a2f90ca9b6b8630da0afbcda5d9f553d4039: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen20144" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20145" type="x-p"/> God reigneth over the heathen - Though this is literally true in God's universal dominion, yet more is here meant. God reigns over the heathen when, by the preaching of the Gospel, they are brought into the Church of Christ. <div eID="gen20145" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20146" type="x-p"/> God sitteth upon the throne of his holiness - He is a holy God; he proclaims holiness. His laws are holy, he requires holiness, and his genuine people are all holy. The throne of his holiness is the heaven of heavens; also the temple at Jerusalem; and, lastly, the hearts of the faithful.
entries.98ac3f355e4dbb77420e78d26c9fb9503b2076ca: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen20146" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20147" type="x-p"/> The princes of the people are gathered together - נדיבי עמים nedibey ammim. The voluntary people - the princely, noble, or free-willed people; those who gladly receive the word of life; those who, like the Bereans, were of a noble or liberal disposition; and, when they heard the Gospel, searched the Scriptures to see whether these things were so. It is a similar word which is used <reference osisRef="Psa.100.3">Psa 100:3</reference>; and I believe both texts speak of the same people - the Gentiles who gladly come unto his light, and present themselves a free-will offering to the Lord. <div eID="gen20147" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20148" type="x-p"/> The people or the God of Abraham - Who were Abraham's people? Not the Jews; the covenant was made with him while yet in urcircumcision. Properly speaking, the Gentiles are those whom he represented; for the covenant was made with him while yet a Gentile; and in his seed all the nations - the Gentiles, of the earth were to be blessed. The people of the God of Abraham are the Gentiles who, receiving the Gospel, are made partakers of the faith of Abraham, and are his spiritual children. The God of Abraham has Abraham's spiritual posterity, the believing Gentiles, for his own people. <div eID="gen20148" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20149" type="x-p"/> The shields of the earth belong unto God - The Septuagint translate this οἱ κραταιοι, the strong ones of the earth. The Vulgate reads, Quoniam dii fortes terrae vehementer elevati sunt; "Because the strong gods of the earth are exceedingly exalted." These are supposed to mean kings and rulers of provinces which were present at the dedication of the temple; (for some suppose the Psalm to have been composed for this solemnity); and that they are said here to be greatly exalted, because they exercised a very high degree of power over their respective districts. The words refer to something by which the inhabitants of the earth are defended; God's providence, guardian angels, etc., etc. <div eID="gen20149" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20150" type="x-p"/> He is greatly exalted - Great as secular rulers are, God is greater, and is above all; King of kings and Lord of lords; and the hearts of kings and governors are in his hand; and he turns them whithersoever he pleases.  <chapter eID="Ps.47"/> <div eID="gen20150" type="x-p"/>

entries.8a340e02ef60e2cf1af344defde70090dcc5a555: <reference osisRef="Ps.47.1-Ps.47.3">Psa 47:1-3</reference> (Hebrew_Bible_47:2-4) “<hi type="italic">Thereupon the fear of Elohim</hi>” - so closes the chronicler (<reference osisRef="2Chr.20.29">2Ch 20:29</reference>) the narrative of the defeat of the confederates -  <hi type="italic">“came upon all kingdoms of the countries, when they heard that Jahve had fought against the enemies of Israel.”</hi> The psalmist, however, does not in consequence or this particular event call upon them to tremble with fear, but to rejoice; for fear is an involuntary, extorted inward emotion, but joy a perfectly voluntary one. The true and final victory of Jahve consists not in a submission that is brought about by war and bloodshed and in consternation that stupefies the mind, but in a change in the minds and hearts of the peoples, so that they render joyful worship unto Him. In order that He may thus become the God of all peoples, He has first of all become the God of Israel; and Israel longs that this the purpose of its election may be attained. Out of this longing springs the call in Psa 47:2. The peoples are to show the God of revelation their joy by their gestures and their words; for Jahve is absolutely exalted (עליון, here it is a predicate, just as in <reference osisRef="Ps.78.56">Psa 78:56</reference> it is an attribute), terrible, and the sphere of His dominion has Israel for its central point, not, however, for its limit, but it extends over the whole earth. Everything must do homage to Him in His own people, whether willingly or by constraint. According to the tenses employed, what is affirmed in <reference osisRef="Ps.47.4">Psa 47:4</reference> appears to be a principle derived from their recent experience, inasmuch as the contemporary fact is not expressed in an historical form, but generalized and idealised. But יבחר, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.47.5">Psa 47:5</reference></hi>, is against this, since the choosing (election) is an act done once for all and not a continued act; we are therefore driven to regard the futures, as in Num 23:7; Jdg 2:1, as a statement of historical facts. Concerning ידבּר, He bent, made to stoop, vid., Psa 18:48. There is now no necessity for altering יבחר into ירחב, and more especially since this is not suited to the fact which has given occasion to the Psalm. On the contrary, יבחר presupposes that in the event of the day God has shown Himself to be a faithful and powerful Lord [<hi type="italic">lit.</hi> feudal Lord] of the land of Israel; the hostile confederation had thought of nothing less than driving Israel entirely out of its inheritance (<reference osisRef="2Chr.20.11">2Ch 20:11</reference>). The Holy Land is called the pride (גּאון) of Jacob, as being the gift of grace of which this, the people of God’s love, can boast. In <reference osisRef="Amos.6.8">Amo 6:8</reference> גאון יעקב has a different meaning (of the sin of pride), and again another sense in <reference osisRef="Nah.2.3">Nah 2:3</reference> (of the glory of all Israel in accordance with the promise); here it is similar to Isa 13:19. את has a conjunctive accent instead of being followed by <hi type="italic">Makkeph</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.60.2">Psa 60:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.3.12">Pro 3:12</reference> (these are the only three instances). The strophe which follows supports the view that the poet, in <reference osisRef="Ps.47.5">Psa 47:5</reference>, has a recent act of God before his mind.
entries.9c620b47f64845ab9f7bf75ea5e359b56482eb9e: <reference osisRef="Ps.47.4-Ps.47.8">Psa 47:4-8</reference> (Hebrew_Bible_47:5-9) The ascent of God presupposes a previous descent, whether it be a manifestation of Himself in order to utter some promise (<reference osisRef="Gen.17.22">Gen 17:22</reference>; Jdg 13:20) or a triumphant execution of judgment (<reference osisRef="Ps.7.8">Psa 7:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.68.19">Psa 68:19</reference>). So here: God has come down to fight on behalf of His people. They return to the Holy City and He to His throne, which is above on Zion, and higher still, is above in heaven. On בּתרוּעה and קול שׁופר cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.98.6">Psa 98:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.15.28">1Ch 15:28</reference>, but more especially <reference osisRef="Amos.2.2">Amo 2:2</reference>; for the “shout” is here the people’s shout of victory, and “the sound of the horn” the clear sound of the horns announcing the victory, with reference to the celebration of the victory in the Valley of praise and the homeward march amidst the clanging music (2Ch 20:26.). The poet, who has this festival of victory before his mind as having recently taken place, desires that the festive sounds may find an unending and boundless echo unto the glory of God. זמּר is first construed with the accusative as in <reference osisRef="Ps.68.33">Psa 68:33</reference>, then with the dative. Concerning משׂכּיל = ᾠδὴ πενυματική (<reference osisRef="Eph.5.19">Eph 5:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.3.16">Col 3:16</reference>), vid., on Psa 32:1. That which excites to songs of praise is Jahve’s dominion of the world which has just been made manifest. מלך is to be taken in just the same historical sense as ἐβασίλευσας, <reference osisRef="Rev.11.15">Rev 11:15</reference>-18. What has taken place is a prelude of the final and visible entering upon the kingdom, the announcement of which the New Testament seer there hears. God has come down to earth, and after having obtained for Himself a recognition of His dominion by the destruction of the enemies of Israel, He has ascended again in visible kingly glory. <hi type="italic">Imago conscensi a Messia throni gloriae</hi>, says Chr. Aug. Crusius, <hi type="italic">tune erat deportatio arcae faederis in sedem regni</hi>.
entries.d43b0734e43762fbc1aad4258eabb7f921a301f8: <reference osisRef="Ps.47.9">Psa 47:9</reference> (Hebrew_Bible_47:10) In the mirror of the present event, the poet reads the great fact of the conversion of all peoples to Jahve which closes the history of the world. The nobles of the peoples (נדיבי with the twofold meaning of <hi type="italic">generosi</hi>), the “shields (i.e., the lords who are the defenders of their people) of the earth” (Hos 4:18), enter into the society of the people of the God of Abraham; πέρας αἱ πρὸς τὸν πατριάρχην Ἀβραὰμ ἔλαβον ὑποσχέσεις, as Theodoret observes. The promise concerning the blessing of the tribes of the nations in the seed of the patriarch is being fulfilled; for the nobles draw the peoples who are protected by them after themselves. It is unnecessary to read עם instead of עם with Ewald, and following the lxx and Syriac; and it is also inadmissible, since one does not say נאסף עם, but ל or אל. Even Eusebius has rightly praised Symmachus and Theodotion, because they have translated the ambiguous ἀμ by λαὸς (τοῦ Θεοῦ Ἀβραάμ), viz., as being a nominative of the effect or result, as it is also understood by the Targum, Jerome, Luther, and most of the Jewish expositors, and among modern expositors by Crusius, Hupfeld, and Hitzig: They gather and band themselves together as a people or into a people of the God of Abraham, they submit themselves with Israel to the one God who is proved to be so glorious.<note placement="foot">It is also accented accordingly, viz., נאספו with <hi type="italic">Rebia magnum</hi>, which (and in this respect it is distinguished from <hi type="italic">Mugrash</hi>) makes a pause; and this is then followed by the supplementing clause with <hi type="italic">Zinnor, Galgal</hi>, and <hi type="italic">Olewejored</hi>.</note> <div eID="gen9494" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9495" type="x-p"/> The conclusion (v. 11) reminds one of the song of Hannah, 1Sa 2:8. Thus universal homage is rendered to Him: He is gone up in triumph, and is in consequence thereof highly exalted (נעלה, <hi type="italic">3rd</hi> <hi type="italic">praet</hi>., the result of consequence of the עלה in <reference osisRef="Ps.47.6">Psa 47:6</reference>). The inaccessibleness of the City of God <div eID="gen9495" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9496" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Ps.48.1-Ps.48.14">Psa 48:1-14</reference> is also a song of thanksgiving for victory. It is connected with <reference osisRef="Ps.46.1-Ps.46.11">Psa 46:1-11</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.47.1-Ps.47.9">Psa 47:1-9</reference> by the fundamental thought of the exaltation of Jahve above the peoples of the earth; but is distinguished from them both in this respect, viz., that, in accordance with the favourite characteristic of Korahitic poetry, the song of thanksgiving for victory has become a song in praise of Jerusalem, the glorious and strong city, protected by God who sits enthroned in it. The historical occasion is the same. The mention of the kings points to an army of confederates; <reference osisRef="Ps.48.10">Psa 48:10</reference> points to the gathering held in the temple before the setting out of the army; and the figurative representation of the hostile powers by the shattered ships of Tarshish does not apply to any period so well as to the time of Jehoshaphat. The points of coincidence between this Psalm (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.48.7">Psa 48:7</reference> with <reference osisRef="Isa.33.14">Isa 33:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.48.8">Psa 48:8</reference> with <reference osisRef="Isa.33.21">Isa 33:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.48.13">Psa 48:13</reference> with <reference osisRef="Isa.33.18">Isa 33:18</reference>; v. 15 with <reference osisRef="Isa.33.22">Isa 33:22</reference>), as well as <reference osisRef="Ps.46.1-Ps.46.11">Psa 46:1-11</reference>, and Isaiah do not prove that he is its author.  <chapter eID="Ps.47"/> <div eID="gen9496" type="x-p"/>

PSALM 47
Some think that this psalm was composed at the time when the temple was dedicated, and the ark of the covenant placed in the sanctuary. But as this is a conjecture which has little to support it, it is better, if I am not mistaken, instead of detaining ourselves with this, to consider the subject-matter of the psalm, and the use to which it ought especially to be applied. It was no doubt appointed for the stated holy assemblies, as may be easily gathered from the whole tenor of the poem; and perhaps it was composed by David, and delivered by him to the Levites, to be sung by them before the temple was built, and when the ark as yet abode in the tabernacle. But whoever was its author, he exhorts not only the Israelites, but also all nations, to worship the only true God. It chiefly magnifies the favor which, according to the state of things at that time, God had graciously vouchsafed to the offspring of Abraham; and salvation to the whole world was to proceed from this source. It however contains, at the same time, a prophecy of the future kingdom of Christ. It teaches that the glory which then shone under the figure of the material sanctuary will diffuse its splendor far and wide; when God himself will cause the beams of his grace to shine into distant lands, that kings and nations may be united into fellowship with the children of Abraham.
To the chief musician of the sons of Korah: A Psalm.
Psalm 47:1-4
1. Clap your hands, all ye peoples: shout unto God with the voice of triumph. 2. For Jehovah is high, terrible, and a great King over all the earth. 3. He hath put in order
“Ou, range.” — Fr. marg. “Or, subdued.”
the people under us, and the nations under our feet. 4. He hath chosen our inheritance for us, the glory of Jacob, whom he loved. Selah.
 
1. Clap your hands, all ye peoples As the Psalmist requires the nations, in token of their joy and of their thanksgiving; to God, to clap their hands, or rather exhorts them to a more than ordinary joy, the vehemence of which breaks forth and manifests itself by external expressions, it is certain that he is here speaking of the deliverance which God had wrought for them. Had God erected among the Gentiles some formidable kingdom, this would rather have deprived all of their courage, and overwhelmed them with despair, than given them matter to sing and leap for joy. Besides, the inspired writer does not here treat of some common or ordinary blessings of God; but of such blessings as will fill the whole world with incredible joy, and stir up the minds of all men to celebrate the praises of God. What he adds a little after, that all nations were brought into subjection to Israel, must, therefore, necessarily be understood not of slavish subjection, but of a subjection which is more excellent, and more to be desired, than all the kingdoms of the world. It would be unnatural for those who are subdued and brought to submit by force and fear to leap for joy. Many nations were tributary to David, and to his son Solomon; but while they were so, they ceased not, at the same time, to murmur, and bore impatiently the yoke which was imposed upon them, so far were they from giving thanks to God with joyful and cheerful hearts.
